topics.name: Chlorine
topics.kicker: Element 17 · The yellow-green halogen that keeps drinking water safe
topics.briefing: Chlorine is a yellow-green, choking gas, yet it protects millions of people by killing germs in drinking water and swimming pools. Carl Wilhelm Scheele first made it in 1774, and Humphry Davy later proved it was an element and named it after the Greek word for “pale green.” It is a halogen that joins sodium to make table salt, and it is the key ingredient in household bleach.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1774, Carl Wilhelm Scheele [“SHAY-luh”] made this element by pouring muriatic acid onto the black mineral pyrolusite [“py-roh-LOO-site”], or manganese dioxide. Scheele noticed that the choking, yellowish-green gas he produced could bleach colored materials.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow-green halogen, element 17, which combines with sodium to make table salt.

tossups.p: Followers of Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-zee-AY”] believed this substance was a compound containing oxygen and called it “oxymuriatic acid,” until Humphry Davy showed in 1810 that it was an element. Davy named it after a Greek word meaning “pale green.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this halogen with atomic number 17, used to disinfect swimming pools.

tossups.p: In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis [“SEM-ul-vyce”] sharply cut deaths from childbed fever at a hospital in Vienna by having doctors wash their hands in a bleaching solution made from lime and this element. This element has the highest electron affinity of any element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow-green gas, a halogen with atomic number 17 that is used in bleach.

tossups.p: In 1908, Jersey City, New Jersey, became the first U.S. city to disinfect its public water supply with this element on a regular basis, a step soon copied across the country. Deaths from typhoid fever dropped sharply in cities that adopted that treatment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a halogen used to keep drinking water and swimming pools clean.

tossups.p: Claude Louis Berthollet [“bair-toh-LAY”] showed in the 1780s that this element could whiten cloth, and a whitening solution made with it at a factory in Javel, near Paris, became famous. French speakers still call that kind of liquid eau de Javel [“oh duh zhah-VEL”].
tossups.r: Household bleach contains sodium hypochlorite, a compound of this element. For 10 points, name this halogen, element 17.

tossups.p: In 1823, Michael Faraday squeezed this element into a liquid by heating crystals of one of its hydrates in a sealed, bent glass tube. This gas is about two and a half times as dense as air, so it sinks and collects in low places.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow-green gas, a halogen that combines with sodium to make table salt.

tossups.p: In 1974, Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland warned that atoms of this element, freed by sunlight from CFCs high in the stratosphere, could destroy the ozone layer. One atom of this element can break down as many as 100,000 ozone molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a yellow-green halogen used to disinfect swimming pools and drinking water.

tossups.p: The strong “pool smell” comes not from this element itself but from irritating compounds that form when it reacts with sweat and urine. Similar compounds form when bleach is mixed with ammonia, which is why those two cleaners should never be combined.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element added to swimming pools and drinking water to kill germs.

tossups.p: About three-quarters of this element’s atoms have a mass number of 35, and about one-quarter have a mass number of 37, so its average atomic mass is about 35.5. Its mass spectrum shows two peaks in a 3-to-1 ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this halogen with atomic number 17, which joins sodium to make table salt.

tossups.p: Surprisingly, this element has the highest electron affinity of any element, releasing more energy than fluorine does when it gains an electron. Its ion, which has a charge of negative one, is the most abundant ion dissolved in seawater.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a yellow-green halogen used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools.

tossups.p: When electricity is passed through brine, or salt water, this element bubbles off at one electrode while hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide form at the other. A large share of the element made this way goes into producing PVC plastic for pipes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this halogen with atomic number 17, which is used to make bleach.

tossups.p: A mixture of hydrogen and this element can sit safely in the dark but explodes in bright sunlight, and Robert Bunsen and Henry Roscoe used that reaction to measure light. The product of that reaction dissolves in water to make the acid found in your stomach.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a yellow-green halogen used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools.

tossups.p: During World War I, German forces released clouds of this heavy, choking gas at the Second Battle of Ypres [“EE-pruh”] in 1915, the first large-scale poison gas attack of the war. Fritz Haber, who later won a Nobel Prize for making ammonia, directed that program.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this yellow-green halogen, element 17, which is used to make drinking water safe.

tossups.p: Each molecule of DDT, the pesticide that Rachel Carson wrote about in _Silent Spring_, contains five atoms of this element. The sweetener sucralose is made by replacing three hydroxyl groups in table sugar with atoms of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, a yellow-green halogen used in bleach and to purify water.

tossups.p: When this element is bubbled through a colorless solution of potassium bromide, the liquid turns orange-brown, because this more reactive halogen pushes bromine out of its compound. Its compound with hydrogen is a gas that makes thick white smoke when it meets ammonia gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 17, which forms table salt when it combines with sodium.

trap.title: Chlorine or chloride?
trap.body: Chloride is the ion (Cl⁻) that chlorine becomes in table salt and seawater, and the two names differ by only two letters, so “chloride” is wrong for an element tossup. Chlorine’s Greek root also shows up in chlorophyll, which contains magnesium and no chlorine at all, and its fellow halogens fluorine and bromine share many of its clues.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element” or “this gas,” say chlorine; say chloride only for “this ion.” Atomic number 17, a yellow-green gas, Scheele, Davy, bleach, and pools mean chlorine; atomic number 9 and Teflon mean fluorine; a reddish-brown liquid means bromine.
trap.line: Real answer line: Chlorine (accept Cl or Cl2; do not accept “chloride”)

topics.name: pH
topics.kicker: How acidic or basic a solution is · Neutral is 7, like pure water
topics.briefing: pH is the number chemists use to say how acidic or basic a solution is: 7 is neutral, like pure water, lower numbers are acidic, like lemon juice at about 2, and higher numbers are basic, like bleach. Each step on the scale means ten times more or fewer hydrogen ions, so lemon juice has about 100,000 times more than pure water. Danish chemist Søren Sørensen invented the scale in 1909 at a brewery’s laboratory in Copenhagen.
topics.answerHtml: pH (accept potential of hydrogen or power of hydrogen; prompt on acidity or hydrogen ion concentration; do not accept “pOH” or “pKa”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1934, Arnold Beckman invented an electronic meter to measure this quantity in lemon juice for a group of California citrus growers, and his company grew into a major maker of lab instruments. Such meters work by sensing the voltage across a thin glass bulb.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number that tells how acidic or basic a solution is, on a scale where 7 is neutral.

tossups.p: Søren Sørensen [“SUR-en-sen”] introduced this measure in 1909 while studying proteins and enzymes at the Carlsberg Laboratory, a research lab in Copenhagen founded by a brewer. He defined it using the negative logarithm of a concentration.
tossups.r: Pure water has a value of 7 on this measure. For 10 points, name this scale that tells how acidic or basic a solution is.

tossups.p: The Henderson–Hasselbalch [“HAH-sul-bahlk”] equation says that for a buffer, this quantity equals the pKa of the weak acid plus the logarithm of the ratio of base to acid. When a buffer holds equal amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base, this quantity equals the pKa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how acidic a solution is, which is 7 for pure water.

tossups.p: Halfway to the equivalence point, when a weak acid is being titrated with a strong base, this quantity equals the acid’s pKa. During a titration, this quantity jumps sharply near the equivalence point, giving an S-shaped curve.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this logarithmic measure of acidity, which runs from about 0 to 14.

tossups.p: Hot pure water is still neutral even though its value of this quantity is lower than that of cold pure water, because water splits into more hydrogen and hydroxide ions as it heats up. At 25 degrees Celsius, the ion product of water is 1.0 times 10 to the negative 14th.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, 7 for pure water at room temperature, that tells how acidic a solution is.

tossups.p: Very concentrated solutions of strong acids can have values of this quantity below zero, and car battery acid, a sulfuric acid solution, has a value near zero. For superacids, which are even stronger, chemists use the Hammett acidity function instead of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this logarithmic measure of acidity, on which pure water scores a 7.

tossups.p: As the oceans absorb carbon dioxide from the air, the average value of this quantity for surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since the 1700s, a change called ocean acidification. That small drop makes seawater roughly 30 percent more acidic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how acidic or basic a solution is, which is 7 for pure water.

tossups.p: Some hydrangea [“hy-DRAIN-juh”] flowers turn blue when grown in soil with a low value of this quantity and pink when the value is high. Gardeners spread lime on soil to raise this quantity and sulfur to lower it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of acidity, on a scale where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic.

tossups.p: A buffer made of carbonic acid and bicarbonate keeps this quantity in human blood between about 7.35 and 7.45. If this quantity in blood falls below that range, a person develops acidosis; if it rises above it, alkalosis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scale, on which 7 is neutral, used to measure how acidic a solution is.

tossups.p: Ordinary rain has a value of this quantity of about 5.6, because carbon dioxide dissolves in it to form carbonic acid. Rain with an even lower value, caused mostly by sulfur and nitrogen oxides from burning fuels, is called acid rain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number that tells how acidic a solution is, which is 7 for pure water.

tossups.p: Red cabbage juice turns red or pink at low values of this quantity and green or yellow at high values, so it can be used to estimate it. Universal indicator shows a whole rainbow of colors as this quantity changes, from red through green to purple.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scale, on which acids score below 7 and bases score above 7, that measures acidity.

tossups.p: At 25 degrees Celsius, this quantity and a similar measure based on hydroxide ions always add up to 14. Phenolphthalein [“fee-nol-THAY-leen”] changes from colorless to pink as this quantity rises past about 8.
tossups.r: Each one-unit drop in this quantity means ten times more hydrogen ions. For 10 points, name this measure of acidity.

tossups.p: Every amino acid has a value of this quantity called its isoelectric point, at which the molecule carries no overall electric charge. Biochemists separate proteins in a gel by differences in that value, a technique called isoelectric focusing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how acidic or basic a solution is, which is 7 when the solution is neutral.

tossups.p: Pepsin, a protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach, works best when this quantity is about 2, while enzymes inside lysosomes work best near 5. Stomach acid gets its low value of this quantity from hydrochloric acid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scale that runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic a solution is.

tossups.p: In 1909, Fritz Haber and Zygmunt Klemensiewicz [“kleh-men-SHEH-vich”] built an early glass electrode, the kind of sensor still used to measure this quantity. The lowercase first letter of this quantity’s name is often said to stand for “power” or “potential.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this logarithmic measure of hydrogen ion concentration, which is 7 for pure water.

Its lowercase first letter is often said to stand for “power” or “potential”

trap.title: The scale, not the acid
trap.body: Nearly every pH clue mentions acids, bases, litmus, indicators, or hydrogen ions, so players blurt “acids” or “hydrogen ions” instead of the measurement itself. Others confuse pH with its cousins pOH, which is based on hydroxide ions, and pKa, which measures how strong an acid is; those are different answers.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this number,” “this quantity,” or “this scale,” answer pH. Even when a clue says the value plus a hydroxide-based measure equals 14, the answer is still pH, not pOH.
trap.line: Real answer line: pH (accept potential of hydrogen or power of hydrogen; prompt on acidity or hydrogen ion concentration; do not accept “pOH” or “pKa”)

topics.name: Electrolysis
topics.kicker: Splitting compounds with electricity · How factories make aluminum and chlorine
topics.dates: Water first split this way in 1800; named in 1834
topics.briefing: Electrolysis uses electricity to force apart compounds that would never split on their own. Pass a current through water and bubbles of hydrogen and oxygen collect at the two electrodes, with twice as much hydrogen as oxygen. Humphry Davy used it in 1807 to isolate potassium and sodium for the first time, and giant factories use it to make most of the world’s aluminum and chlorine.
topics.answerHtml: Electrolysis (accept word forms like electrolyze; prompt on electrolytic cell or electrochemistry; do not accept “electrolytes” or “electrodes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Soon after Alessandro Volta announced his pile, a stack of metal disks that made a steady electric current, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle used one to carry out this process on water. That 1800 experiment helped launch the science of electrochemistry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which uses an electric current to split compounds such as water into hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: A Hofmann voltameter [“vohl-TAM-ih-ter”], an upright glass apparatus with three connected tubes, collects the two gases made by this process in separate arms. The gas from one arm relights a glowing splint, while the gas from the other arm burns with a squeaky pop.
tossups.r: Twice as much gas collects above the negative electrode as above the positive one. For 10 points, name this process that splits water with an electric current.

tossups.p: One of Michael Faraday’s laws of this process says that the same amount of charge produces masses of different elements in proportion to their molar masses divided by the charges on their ions. His other law says that the mass produced at an electrode is proportional to the total charge passed.
tossups.r: Humphry Davy used this process to isolate sodium and potassium. For 10 points, name this process in which an electric current breaks compounds apart.

tossups.p: In October 1807, Humphry Davy reportedly danced around his laboratory when tiny globules of a new metal appeared and burst into flame as he performed this process on caustic potash. Days later, he used the same method on caustic soda to isolate a second new metal.
tossups.r: He powered it with a huge battery at the Royal Institution. For 10 points, name this process, which uses electricity to split compounds such as water into hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: In 1886, Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult [“ay-ROO”] in France independently found a way to apply this process to aluminum oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. Their method made aluminum, once about as costly as silver, cheap enough for everyday objects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses an electric current to split compounds, such as water into hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: The chloralkali process uses this method on brine, or salt water: chlorine gas bubbles off at one electrode, while hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide form at the other. Much of the chlorine made this way goes into PVC plastic for pipes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that uses electricity to drive chemical reactions that would not happen on their own.

tossups.p: After several chemists were poisoned or injured trying, Henri Moissan [“mwah-SAHN”] finally isolated fluorine in 1886 by using this process in a chilled platinum apparatus. That work earned him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
tossups.r: Humphry Davy discovered several metals with this process. For 10 points, name this method of splitting compounds with an electric current.

tossups.p: To purify copper, a thick slab of impure copper is made the positive electrode in this process, and nearly pure copper builds up on a thin sheet at the negative electrode. Silver and gold that were mixed into the copper collect in the “anode mud” at the bottom of the tank.
tossups.r: This process is also used to electroplate objects. For 10 points, name this process in which an electric current drives a chemical change.

tossups.p: In a Downs cell, calcium chloride is mixed into melted sodium chloride to lower its melting point before this process splits the salt into liquid sodium metal and chlorine gas. Solid salt will not work, because its ions cannot move until it is melted or dissolved.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, which uses an electric current to break compounds into simpler substances.

tossups.p: In 1808, Humphry Davy used this process to isolate four new metals: calcium, magnesium, strontium, and barium. A year earlier, he had isolated potassium and sodium the same way, using a giant battery at London’s Royal Institution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, in which an electric current splits compounds, such as water into hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: In a cell built for this process, positive ions drift toward the negatively charged cathode, where they gain electrons, while negative ions give up electrons at the positively charged anode. Such a cell needs an outside power source, because its reaction is not spontaneous, unlike the reaction in a galvanic cell.
tossups.r: This process can coat objects with a thin layer of silver or chrome. For 10 points, name this process that uses an electric current to break down compounds.

tossups.p: In a classic school demonstration of this process, melted lead(II) bromide gives off brown bromine vapor at one graphite rod while molten lead collects beneath the other. Graphite is often chosen for those rods because it conducts electricity but does not react.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, in which an electric current splits a compound into simpler substances.

tossups.p: Before this process is carried out on water, a little sulfuric acid is often added, because pure water conducts electricity very poorly. “Green” hydrogen fuel is made by this process using electricity from wind turbines or solar panels.
tossups.r: The gas made at the cathode takes up twice the volume of the gas made at the anode. For 10 points, name this process that splits water using electricity.

tossups.p: Robert Bunsen used banks of his cheap carbon battery cells to make magnesium by this process, and with Augustus Matthiessen he used it to make lithium metal in larger amounts. In both cases, the process was run on the metal’s melted chloride.
tossups.r: Humphry Davy used this process to isolate potassium. For 10 points, name this process, also used to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: Michael Faraday introduced this term in 1834, building it from Greek roots meaning “amber” and “loosening.” With help from William Whewell [“HYOO-el”], Faraday also introduced the words anode and cathode for the two conductors used in this process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, in which an electric current splits compounds, such as water into hydrogen and oxygen.

trap.title: Process, not the parts
trap.body: Electrolysis, electrolytes, and electrodes all come from Michael Faraday’s 1834 vocabulary, and clues about batteries, ions, and splitting water fit all three. Electrolysis is the process; electrolytes are the substances whose ions carry electric charge; electrodes are the conductors where electricity goes in and out. Saying “electrolytic cell” names the container, which earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this process” or “this method” that uses electricity to split compounds, say electrolysis. “These substances” that conduct when dissolved are electrolytes, and “these conductors,” the anode and cathode, are electrodes. A battery that makes electricity from a spontaneous reaction is a galvanic cell, which does the opposite job.
trap.line: Real answer line: Electrolysis (accept word forms like electrolyze; prompt on electrolytic cell or electrochemistry; do not accept “electrolytes” or “electrodes”)

topics.name: Gold
topics.kicker: Element 79, the most malleable metal · Treasured for thousands of years
topics.briefing: Gold is the soft, shiny yellow metal that people have treasured for thousands of years, from the funeral mask of King Tutankhamun to modern wedding rings. Its symbol, Au, comes from the Latin word aurum, and it is the most malleable metal: one gram can be hammered into a sheet about a meter on each side. Because it does not rust or tarnish, gold from ancient tombs still shines.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1980, Glenn Seaborg’s team used a particle accelerator to turn several thousand atoms of bismuth into this element, a feat that cost far more than the product was worth. Alchemists linked this metal with the Sun.
tossups.r: Alchemists also sought a “philosopher’s stone” that could turn lead into this metal. For 10 points, name this precious element with atomic number 79.

tossups.p: In the 1920s, Fritz Haber spent years trying to pull this element out of seawater to help Germany pay its World War I reparations, but the oceans held far less of it than earlier measurements had suggested.
tossups.r: This metal’s symbol comes from the Latin word aurum. For 10 points, name this precious yellow element with atomic number 79.

tossups.p: In 1940, as German troops occupied Copenhagen, George de Hevesy [“HEV-eh-shee”] hid two Nobel Prize medals from the Nazis by dissolving them in aqua regia, a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acids that can dissolve this metal. The metal was later recovered and the medals were recast.
tossups.r: This metal does not tarnish, and it resists most other acids. For 10 points, name this precious metal, element number 79.

tossups.p: The Roman Lycurgus [“ly-KUR-gus”] Cup looks green in reflected light but glows red when lit from behind, because its glass holds tiny particles of silver and this metal. In 1857, Michael Faraday made a ruby-red liquid holding specks of this metal far too small to see.
tossups.r: Pure samples of this metal are called 24-karat. For 10 points, name this precious yellow metal, element number 79.

tossups.p: Einstein’s theory of relativity helps explain this metal’s color: electrons in its heavy atoms move so fast that their energies shift, so the metal absorbs blue light and reflects yellow. Sheets of this metal thin enough to see through let greenish-blue light pass.
tossups.r: One gram of this most malleable metal can be hammered into a sheet about a square meter in size. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 79.

tossups.p: In 2017, astronomers studied the glow from a collision of two neutron stars that gravitational-wave detectors had picked up, and found signs that such crashes forge this element and other heavy metals. On Earth, this element has only one stable isotope, with mass number 197.
tossups.r: Its chemical symbol comes from the Latin aurum. For 10 points, name this precious yellow metal, found at Sutter’s Mill in 1848.

tossups.p: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin foil of this metal in 1909 and saw a few of them bounce almost straight back. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford used their results to discover the atomic nucleus.
tossups.r: That foil could be made very thin because this element is the most malleable metal. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 79.

tossups.p: Many rapid home tests, including some for COVID-19, form their colored result line from nanoparticles of this metal, which look red instead of yellow. Electronics makers coat connectors with this metal because it conducts electricity well and does not corrode.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this precious metal whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word aurum.

tossups.p: Each of the 18 hexagonal mirror segments of the James Webb Space Telescope is coated with a very thin layer of this metal, which reflects infrared light extremely well. Spacesuit helmet visors are also coated with this metal to block harsh sunlight.
tossups.r: King Midas could turn whatever he touched into this metal. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 79.

tossups.p: Mixing this metal with copper makes a “rose” alloy, and mixing it with nickel or palladium makes a “white” alloy. Jewelers measure this metal’s purity in karats, so an 18-karat ring is 75 percent this metal, while a 24-karat ring is pure.
tossups.r: Its atomic number is 79, between platinum and mercury. For 10 points, name this precious yellow metal.

tossups.p: Large mines dissolve this metal out of crushed ore using a cyanide solution, while some small-scale miners use mercury, which grabs this metal to form an amalgam and pollutes rivers. This metal is about 19 times as dense as water.
tossups.r: Prospectors panned for it in California after 1848. For 10 points, name this precious metal, element number 79.

tossups.p: Counterfeiters have hidden bars of tungsten inside fake bars of this metal, because the two metals have almost the same density. This metal’s price is usually quoted per troy ounce, which is about 31.1 grams.
tossups.r: Fort Knox in Kentucky stores much of the U.S. government’s supply of this metal. For 10 points, name this precious metal, element number 79.

tossups.p: To win his freedom from Francisco Pizarro, the Inca ruler Atahualpa [“ah-tah-WAHL-pah”] promised to fill a room once with this metal and twice with silver. Spanish explorers also searched for El Dorado, a legendary ruler said to be covered in dust of this metal.
tossups.r: This element is number 79 on the periodic table. For 10 points, name this precious yellow metal.

tossups.p: A discovery of this metal on the Witwatersrand [“WIT-wah-terz-rand”] in 1886 led to the founding of Johannesburg, South Africa. Ten years later, a find of this metal in Canada’s Yukon region set off the Klondike stampede.
tossups.r: James Marshall’s 1848 discovery of this metal at Sutter’s Mill drew the “forty-niners” to California. For 10 points, name this metal, element number 79.

tossups.p: During his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali gave away so much of this metal in Cairo that its value there fell for years. The funeral mask of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun [“too-tahn-KAH-mun”] is made mostly of this metal.
tossups.r: This metal does not rust or tarnish, so ancient objects made of it still shine. For 10 points, name this precious metal, element number 79.

trap.title: Not fool’s gold
trap.body: Pyrite, a shiny brass-colored compound of iron and sulfur, is nicknamed “fool’s gold,” and real answer lines do not accept it. Gold also shares its column of the periodic table with copper and silver, so clues about coins, jewelry, or precious metals can fit silver or platinum too. Saying “Au” is fine, but naming a compound like “gold chloride” is wrong when the question asks for the element.
trap.fix: Atomic number 79, the Latin aurum, Sutter’s Mill, aqua regia, the most malleable metal, and Rutherford’s foil mean gold. Iron and sulfur, or crystals shaped like cubes, mean pyrite; atomic number 47, tarnishing, and the Latin argentum mean silver; atomic number 78 and catalytic converters mean platinum.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gold (accept Au; do not accept “fool’s gold” or “pyrite”)

topics.name: Flame test
topics.kicker: Identifying metals by flame color · The chemistry behind colored fireworks
topics.dates: Studied with the spectroscope by Bunsen and Kirchhoff from 1859
topics.briefing: In a flame test, a chemist dips a clean wire loop into a sample and holds it in a hot, nearly invisible blue flame to see what color appears. Many metals give their own colors: sodium glows yellow-orange, potassium lilac, copper green or blue-green, and strontium bright red. Heat bumps electrons up to higher energy levels, and as they fall back, they give off light of particular colors, the same chemistry that colors fireworks.
topics.answerHtml: Flame test (prompt on spectroscopy, emission spectroscopy, or flame photometry; do not accept “Bunsen burner”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1861, William Crookes discovered thallium by spotting a bright green line in the light from a heated sample, and he named the element from a Greek word for a green shoot. Chemists use colors like that one in this simple lab test, which can tell barium’s pale green from copper’s blue-green.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the color they give off when heated in a burner.

tossups.p: In 1860, Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff [“KEER-kof”] boiled down huge amounts of mineral water and found a new element by two bright blue lines in its light, naming it cesium, from the Latin for “sky blue.” Their spectroscope used a prism to spread out the colored light seen in this test.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test, in which a sample is held in a flame to identify metals by color.

tossups.p: Chemists checking for potassium in this test often look through blue cobalt glass, which blocks the glare of sodium, because even a trace of sodium can hide other colors. Through the glass, potassium’s pale violet, or lilac, color shows up.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the colors they give off when heated in a burner.

tossups.p: Before this test, a loop of platinum or nichrome [“NYE-krohm”] wire is dipped in hydrochloric acid and heated again and again until it adds no color of its own. Some teachers instead soak wooden splints in the solutions being tested.
tossups.r: Next, the sample is held in a hot, nearly colorless flame. For 10 points, name this test that identifies metals by the color they give off.

tossups.p: Chemists often use the chloride salts of metals in this test, because chlorides turn into vapor easily in a hot flame and give brighter colors. The color comes from the metal ions, not from the chloride, so sodium chloride and sodium nitrate give the same yellow-orange glow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this test that identifies metals by the colors they give off when heated.

tossups.p: Compounds of boron, such as boric acid mixed with methanol, burn with a bright green color, so this test can also detect borates. Barium compounds give a paler, apple-green color in the same test.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test in which samples are heated in a flame to identify elements by color.

tossups.p: Blue is the hardest color for fireworks makers to produce, because the copper compounds that give it break down if the burning mixture gets too hot. Fireworks use the same chemistry as this lab test, with strontium salts for red and barium salts for green.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the colors they give off in a flame.

tossups.p: One of Gustav Kirchhoff’s [“KEER-kofs”] three laws of spectroscopy says that a hot, thin gas gives off light only at certain colors, which show up as bright lines through a prism. Those bright lines explain the colors seen in this test, such as strontium’s bright red.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this test in which a metal’s compounds are heated in a burner to identify the metal by color.

tossups.p: This test works because heat bumps electrons up to higher energy levels, and when they fall back down, they give off light whose color matches the exact energy difference. Every element has its own set of energy levels, so each gives its own pattern of colors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by heating them in a burner and watching the color.

tossups.p: This test works best with a burner whose air hole is open, giving a hot, nearly invisible blue flame that does not add a yellow glow of its own. The university mechanic Peter Desaga [“deh-ZAH-gah”] built the most famous burner of that kind in 1855.
tossups.r: That burner is named for Robert Bunsen. For 10 points, name this test that identifies metals by the color they give a flame.

tossups.p: The bright yellow-orange color that sodium gives in this test comes mostly from two close lines near 589 nanometers, which match the dark lines in sunlight that Joseph von Fraunhofer [“FROWN-hoh-fer”] labeled D. Streetlights filled with sodium vapor glow the same color.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the color they give off when heated in a flame.

tossups.p: An instrument called a flame photometer measures how much sodium or potassium is in a sample, while this simpler test only shows which metals are present. In this simpler test, calcium compounds give a brick-red or orange-red color, and copper compounds give a green or blue-green one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by heating samples in a burner’s flame.

tossups.p: In qualitative analysis, this test is used to identify positive metal ions, while negative ions like chloride are found with other tests, such as adding silver nitrate to make a white precipitate. Not every metal gives a color in this test; magnesium compounds, for example, give none.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this test that identifies metals, like sodium and potassium, by the colors they give off when heated.

tossups.p: When salty pasta water boils over onto a gas stove, the burner’s blue flame flashes yellow-orange, an everyday example of this test’s chemistry. In this test, potassium gives lilac, lithium gives crimson, and barium gives pale green.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the colors they give off in a flame.

tossups.p: In 1818, Christian Gmelin [“GMAY-leen”] noticed that salts of lithium, an element discovered the year before, give a bright red color in this test. Strontium gives a similar red, which is why its nitrate is used in highway road flares.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lab test that identifies metals by the colors they give off in a burner’s flame.

trap.title: Element or the test?
trap.body: Flame colors show up in tossups about single elements too: a lilac flame means potassium, a yellow-orange one means sodium, and a crimson one can mean lithium or strontium. On this answer line, the question wants the procedure itself, so naming the element, the Bunsen burner, or fireworks is wrong, and the broader method, “spectroscopy,” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun at the end. “This test” or “this procedure” wants the flame test; “this element” wants the metal whose color is described; “this device” or “this burner” wants the Bunsen burner. If you are prompted after saying “spectroscopy,” narrow it to the flame test.
trap.line: Real answer line: Flame test (prompt on spectroscopy, emission spectroscopy, or flame photometry; do not accept “Bunsen burner”)

topics.name: Diels–Alder reaction
topics.kicker: Diene plus dienophile makes a ring · Earned its discoverers a 1950 Nobel Prize
topics.briefing: The Diels–Alder reaction snaps two molecules together into a six-membered ring in a single step. One partner, the diene, has two double bonds; the other, the dienophile, usually has one. German chemists Otto Diels and his former student Kurt Alder first described it in 1928 and shared the 1950 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and chemists still use it to build complicated molecules, from medicines to plastics.
topics.answerHtml: Diels–Alder reaction (accept Diels–Alder cycloaddition or diene synthesis; prompt on cycloaddition, [4+2] cycloaddition, or pericyclic reaction)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The insecticides aldrin and dieldrin, both made using this reaction and later banned in many countries, were named after the two chemists who discovered it. This reaction makes two new carbon–carbon single bonds in one step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction in which a diene and a dienophile join to form a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: Kenichi Fukui [“foo-KOO-ee”] and Roald Hoffmann shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for explaining how reactions like this one take place. Fukui’s frontier orbital theory says this reaction depends on the highest occupied orbital of one reactant overlapping the lowest unoccupied orbital of the other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction in which a diene and a dienophile join to form a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: The Woodward–Hoffmann rules use orbital symmetry to show that this reaction is “thermally allowed,” so heat alone can make it go. The same rules explain why joining two alkenes into a four-membered ring needs light instead of heat.
tossups.r: This reaction’s namesakes won the 1950 Nobel Prize. For 10 points, name this [4+2] cycloaddition between a diene and a dienophile.

tossups.p: Bottles of cyclopentadiene [“sy-kloh-pen-tuh-DY-een”] slowly turn into dicyclopentadiene at room temperature, because the compound undergoes this reaction with itself. Chemists get fresh cyclopentadiene back by heating the dimer, which runs this reaction in reverse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction in which a diene and a dienophile combine to make a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: This reaction was first described in 1928 by a chemistry professor at the University of Kiel [“KEEL”] and his former doctoral student. One of its two partners has a name meaning “diene-loving,” because it readily joins a molecule that has two double bonds.
tossups.r: Those German chemists shared the 1950 Nobel Prize for it. For 10 points, name this reaction between a diene and a dienophile.

tossups.p: In a common college teaching lab, anthracene is heated with maleic anhydride, a very reactive partner for this reaction, to make a new ring bridging the middle of anthracene. Maleic anhydride works well because its carbonyl groups pull electrons away from its double bond.
tossups.r: It forms a six-membered ring in one step. For 10 points, name this cycloaddition between a diene and a dienophile.

tossups.p: For this reaction to work, its four-carbon partner must twist into an s-cis shape, with both of its double bonds on the same side of the single bond that joins them. Molecules locked into the opposite, s-trans shape cannot react this way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction between a diene and a dienophile that makes cyclohexene rings.

tossups.p: When a cyclic partner reacts this way, the “endo” product, with the two-carbon partner’s groups tucked under the four-carbon partner, usually forms faster than the “exo” product. This reaction is stereospecific, so groups that start out cis on the two-carbon partner stay cis in the product.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction in which a diene and a dienophile form a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: In “hetero” versions of this reaction, an atom other than carbon, such as oxygen or nitrogen, becomes part of the new ring. Lewis acids such as aluminum chloride can speed up this reaction by pulling electrons away from one of the partners.
tossups.r: It joins a diene and a dienophile. For 10 points, name this [4+2] cycloaddition, named for two Nobel-winning German chemists.

tossups.p: If the two-carbon partner in this reaction is an alkyne instead of an alkene, the product ring keeps two double bonds and is called a cyclohexadiene [“sy-kloh-hex-uh-DY-een”]. With an ordinary alkene partner, the ring keeps just one double bond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction, in which a diene and a dienophile join to make a cyclohexene ring.

tossups.p: In one step, this reaction breaks three pi bonds and forms two new sigma bonds and one new pi bond, with no intermediate along the way. Because all of those bonds change at the same time, chemists call it a concerted reaction.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction that combines a diene and a dienophile into a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: When the four-carbon and two-carbon parts sit on the same molecule, an intramolecular version of this reaction can build two rings at once. Chemists use such steps to build complex natural products that contain several rings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction, in which a diene and a dienophile form a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: Some self-healing plastics are held together by links made through this reaction between furan [“FYOOR-an”] and maleimide [“muh-LAY-ih-mide”] groups. Heating such a plastic breaks the links by running this reaction in reverse, and cooling lets them form again, mending cracks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction between a diene and a dienophile that forms a six-membered ring.

tossups.p: Along with electrocyclic reactions and sigmatropic shifts like the Cope rearrangement, this reaction is a pericyclic reaction, in which electrons flow around a ring of atoms in a single step. Unlike those reactions, this one usually joins two separate molecules into one ring.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reaction between a diene and a dienophile, named for two German chemists.

tossups.p: The simplest textbook example of this reaction joins two small hydrocarbons, but it is slow and needs high heat and pressure. In its product, the single bond that was in the middle of the four-carbon reactant becomes a double bond.
tossups.r: That example makes cyclohexene from butadiene and ethylene. For 10 points, name this [4+2] cycloaddition, whose discoverers won a 1950 Nobel Prize.

The insecticides aldrin and dieldrin, made using it and later banned in many countries, were named for its discoverers

The Woodward–Hoffmann rules show it is “thermally allowed”; joining two alkenes into a four-membered ring needs light instead

trap.title: Name the whole reaction
trap.body: Tossups on this reaction are full of its parts, so players blurt “diene,” “dienophile,” or “cyclohexene,” which are reactants or products, not the reaction. Saying only “cycloaddition” or “[4+2] cycloaddition” earns a prompt, and the Alder–ene reaction, named for just one of the two chemists, is a different answer. The similar-sounding aldol reaction is unrelated.
trap.fix: When you hear a four-carbon partner with two double bonds, a dienophile, s-cis, endo, or a new six-membered ring made in one step, say “Diels–Alder.” If you are prompted after “cycloaddition,” add the two names. Two carbonyl compounds joining through an enolate mean the aldol reaction instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Diels–Alder reaction (accept Diels–Alder cycloaddition or diene synthesis; prompt on cycloaddition, [4+2] cycloaddition, or pericyclic reaction)

topics.name: Linus Pauling
topics.kicker: American chemist of the chemical bond · The only winner of two unshared Nobels
topics.briefing: Linus Pauling was an American chemist who explained how atoms hold together in molecules, using the new ideas of quantum physics. He created the first electronegativity scale, proposed the alpha helix shape found in many proteins, and won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. He later campaigned against nuclear weapons tests and won the 1962 Nobel Peace Prize, making him the only person to win two Nobel Prizes that he did not share with anyone.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While sick in bed with a cold in Oxford in 1948, this scientist drew a chain of amino acids on a sheet of paper and folded it until he found a spiral shape that fit. With Robert Corey, he later published that shape, the alpha helix, along with the beta pleated sheet.
tossups.r: He also made the best-known electronegativity scale. For 10 points, name this American chemist who won Nobel Prizes for Chemistry and for Peace.

tossups.p: With Emile Zuckerkandl [“TSOO-ker-kahn-dl”], this scientist proposed the idea of a “molecular clock,” in which changes in proteins such as hemoglobin pile up at a roughly steady rate and can be used to estimate when species split apart. Earlier, his team called sickle-cell anemia a “molecular disease.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this chemist who won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the 1962 Nobel Peace Prize.

tossups.p: This scientist’s five rules, published in 1929, predict how positive and negative ions pack together in crystals such as minerals. His first published research used X-rays to work out the crystal structure of the mineral molybdenite [“muh-LIB-duh-nite”].
tossups.r: He won two Nobel Prizes, neither of them shared. For 10 points, name this American chemist who created the most widely used electronegativity scale.

tossups.p: This scientist explained why ordinary ice keeps some entropy even near absolute zero: its hydrogen atoms can be arranged in a huge number of ways. He also showed that orbitals on one atom can mix into hybrids, such as the four sp³ hybrids on the carbon atom in methane.
tossups.r: This American won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry and Peace. For 10 points, name this author of _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_.

tossups.p: In 1958, this scientist, with help from his wife, Ava Helen, gave the United Nations a petition signed by thousands of scientists from around the world, calling for an end to nuclear weapons tests. That same year, he published the book _No More War!_
tossups.r: His campaign earned him a Nobel Peace Prize, his second Nobel. For 10 points, name this American chemist.

tossups.p: In 1952, the U.S. government refused this scientist a passport for months, keeping him from a scientific meeting in London. Early the next year, he and Robert Corey proposed a three-stranded model of DNA, which turned out to be wrong when James Watson and Francis Crick published the double helix.
tossups.r: This American chemist also proposed the alpha helix shape of proteins. For 10 points, name this winner of two unshared Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: In 1949, this scientist’s team, including Harvey Itano [“ih-TAH-noh”], used electrophoresis to show that the hemoglobin of people with sickle-cell anemia carries a different electric charge than normal hemoglobin. Their paper called the condition a “molecular disease,” the first ever identified.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American chemist who won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on chemical bonds.

tossups.p: This scientist coined the term “orthomolecular medicine,” and an institute named for him is at Oregon State University, where he went to college. In 1970, he wrote a bestseller promoting large doses of vitamin C against the common cold, a claim many doctors disputed.
tossups.r: He won his first Nobel Prize for studying chemical bonds. For 10 points, name this chemist, the only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: This scientist used the idea of resonance to explain why all six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene are the same length, picturing the real molecule as a blend of two structures. In 1932, he built the first scale of electronegativity, on which fluorine has the highest value.
tossups.r: He wrote _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_. For 10 points, name this American chemist who also won the 1962 Nobel Peace Prize.

tossups.p: As a young Guggenheim fellow in 1926 and 1927, this scientist studied the new quantum mechanics in Europe with Arnold Sommerfeld in Munich, Niels Bohr in Copenhagen, and Erwin Schrödinger [“SHROH-ding-er”] in Zurich. He then spent most of his career at Caltech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this chemist who explained chemical bonding with quantum ideas, the author of _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_.

tossups.p: This scientist’s second Nobel Prize was announced on October 10, 1963, the same day that the Partial Test Ban Treaty went into effect. That treaty banned nuclear weapons tests in the air, in outer space, and underwater, the kind of ban he had campaigned for.
tossups.r: That Peace Prize joined a Chemistry Prize he had won in 1954. For 10 points, name this American, the only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: This scientist’s 1939 book, which grew out of a series of papers he began publishing in 1931, became one of the most influential chemistry books of the 20th century. In it, he explained bonding using quantum mechanics and his own ideas of resonance and orbital hybridization.
tossups.r: That book is _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_. For 10 points, name this chemist who won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

tossups.p: This scientist grew up in Portland, Oregon, where his father, a druggist, died when he was nine. He studied chemical engineering at Oregon Agricultural College, where he met his future wife, Ava Helen Miller, before earning his doctorate at Caltech in 1925.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American chemist who won Nobel Prizes in both Chemistry and Peace.

tossups.p: This scientist built his best-known scale by measuring how much stronger a bond between two different atoms is than expected from bonds between like atoms. On that scale, hydrogen is listed at 2.20, and fluorine tops the chart at nearly 4.
tossups.r: That scale measures electronegativity. For 10 points, name this American chemist who won two unshared Nobel Prizes.

tossups.p: This scientist is the P in CPK, the name for a popular set of space-filling molecular models and for the common color code in which carbon atoms are black, oxygen red, and nitrogen blue. The C stands for his longtime partner Robert Corey.
tossups.r: He proposed the alpha helix. For 10 points, name this American chemist, the only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes.

In 1958, with help from his wife, Ava Helen, he gave the UN a petition from thousands of scientists to end nuclear tests; he wrote _No More War!_

trap.title: Pauling or Pauli?
trap.body: Linus Pauling and Wolfgang Pauli have nearly the same name and both used quantum ideas about electrons, but Pauli was an Austrian physicist known for the exclusion principle. The two-Nobel clue also tempts players to say Marie Curie, who won two Nobels but shared one of them, and Robert Mulliken made a different electronegativity scale.
trap.fix: Electronegativity on a scale where fluorine is nearly 4, the alpha helix, _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_, vitamin C, sickle cell, and the Peace Prize mean Pauling. “No two electrons in an atom share all four quantum numbers” means Pauli; radioactivity, polonium, and radium mean Curie; molecular orbitals mean Mulliken.

topics.name: Electrodes
topics.kicker: Where current enters and leaves · Every cell’s anode and cathode
topics.briefing: Electrodes are the conductors where electric current enters or leaves a battery, an electrolysis tank, or even a patient’s skin during a heart test. An electrochemical cell needs two: oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode, and positive ions drift toward the cathode. Michael Faraday introduced the word in 1834 from Greek roots meaning “amber” and “way.”
topics.answerHtml: Electrodes (accept electrode; prompt on terminals or conductors; do not accept “anode,” “cathode,” “electrons,” or “electrolytes”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Willem Einthoven [“AYNT-hoh-ven”] won the 1924 Nobel Prize in Medicine for recording the heart’s electrical activity, and a triangle named for him connects three of these conductors placed on the right arm, left arm, and left leg. A standard 12-lead heart tracing uses ten of them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, which come in anode and cathode types, where current enters or leaves a battery or a solution.

tossups.p: In 1924, Hans Berger recorded the first human brain waves by attaching these conductors to a person’s head, inventing the EEG. Defibrillator pads, which deliver a shock that can reset a dangerous heart rhythm, are also large versions of these conductors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors where electric current enters or leaves, called anodes and cathodes in batteries.

tossups.p: Chemists assign exactly zero volts to a standard hydrogen one of these, made of platinum dipped in an acid solution with hydrogen gas bubbling over it. Other half-cells are ranked by comparing their voltages to it.
tossups.r: Oxidation happens at one kind of them and reduction at the other. For 10 points, name these conductors, such as the anode and cathode of a battery.

tossups.p: The saturated calomel [“KAL-uh-mel”] type of these conductors uses mercury in contact with mercury(I) chloride, while a silver–silver chloride type is a common mercury-free choice. Both are used as references against which other voltages are measured.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, called anodes and cathodes, through which current enters or leaves an electrolyte.

tossups.p: In 1909, Fritz Haber and Zygmunt Klemensiewicz [“kleh-men-SHEH-vich”] built an early glass one of these conductors, the kind still used in pH meters. A pH meter compares the voltage of that glass one with the voltage of a reference one.
tossups.r: Michael Faraday introduced their name in 1834. For 10 points, name these conductors, such as the anode and cathode in a battery.

tossups.p: John Goodenough shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for finding that lithium cobalt oxide makes an excellent positive one of these in rechargeable batteries. In a lithium-ion battery, the negative one is usually made of graphite.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, called anodes and cathodes, where current enters or leaves a battery.

tossups.p: In the Daniell cell, invented in 1836, a zinc one of these sits in zinc sulfate solution and a copper one sits in copper(II) sulfate solution, with a porous barrier between them. The zinc one slowly dissolves as it gives up electrons.
tossups.r: The zinc one is the anode, and the copper one is the cathode. For 10 points, name these conductors where current enters or leaves an electrochemical cell.

tossups.p: In 1859, Gaston Planté [“plahn-TAY”] invented the first rechargeable battery, using two lead sheets as these conductors in sulfuric acid. In a car battery of that type, one set of these plates is lead and the other is lead dioxide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, which include the anode and cathode of a battery.

tossups.p: Michael Faraday introduced this word in 1834, building it from Greek roots meaning “amber” and “way,” and with help from William Whewell [“HYOO-el”] he named its two kinds. Faraday’s laws say the mass of metal deposited on one of these depends on the charge that flows.
tossups.r: Those two kinds are the anode and cathode. For 10 points, name these conductors where current enters or leaves a solution during electrolysis.

tossups.p: Electric arc furnaces melt scrap steel with giant arcs that jump from huge graphite versions of these conductors into the metal. In aluminum smelters, the positive carbon ones slowly burn away as they react with oxygen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, the anodes and cathodes where current enters or leaves.

tossups.p: Blocks of zinc or magnesium bolted to ship hulls act as “sacrificial” versions of these conductors, corroding in place of the steel, a method called cathodic protection. Many home water heaters hold a magnesium rod that works the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, called anodes or cathodes depending on whether oxidation or reduction happens at them.

tossups.p: Lee de Forest added a third one of these conductors, a wire grid, to a vacuum tube to create the Audion, which could amplify signals. In such tubes, a heated one of these conductors gives off electrons that fly toward a positive plate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, such as anodes and cathodes, where current enters or leaves a device.

tossups.p: A car’s spark plug has two of these conductors with a tiny gap between them, where a spark lights the fuel mixture. In arc welding, a metal rod that serves as one of these melts to help join two pieces of metal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, called anodes and cathodes in batteries and in electrolysis.

tossups.p: In electroplating, the object to be coated is made the negative one of these conductors, so metal ions in the solution gain electrons and coat it. Platinum and graphite are popular choices for these conductors because they do not react.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these conductors, the anode and cathode, where current enters or leaves an electrolyte.

tossups.p: In a hydrogen fuel cell, hydrogen gas gives up electrons at one of these conductors, while oxygen gas takes in electrons at the other, and a plastic membrane between them lets only protons through. Both of these conductors are usually coated with a platinum catalyst.
tossups.r: In any cell, positive ions drift toward the cathode. For 10 points, name these conductors, called the anode and the cathode.

trap.title: Electrodes, not electrons
trap.body: “Electrodes” sounds almost like “electrons,” and both show up in battery clues, but electrons are the particles that flow, while electrodes are the conductors they flow into and out of. Electrolytes are the substances between the electrodes, and electrolysis is the process some electrodes drive. Naming just one kind, “anode” or “cathode,” is wrong when the question asks for the whole group.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these conductors” that come in anode and cathode types, say electrodes. “These particles” with a negative charge are electrons; “these substances” that conduct when dissolved are electrolytes; “this process” that splits compounds with electricity is electrolysis.
trap.line: Real answer line: Electrodes (accept electrode; prompt on terminals or conductors; do not accept “anode,” “cathode,” “electrons,” or “electrolytes”)

topics.name: Gas constant
topics.kicker: The R in PV = nRT · About 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin
topics.briefing: The gas constant, written R, is the number that makes the ideal gas law work: pressure times volume equals moles times R times temperature. It equals about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, or about 0.0821 liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin, and it is really Boltzmann’s constant scaled up to a whole mole. R also turns up in equations for reaction rates, battery voltages, and chemical equilibrium.
topics.answerHtml: Gas constant (accept R, ideal gas constant, universal gas constant, or molar gas constant; do not accept “Boltzmann constant” or “Avogadro’s number”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The law of Dulong [“doo-LONG”] and Petit [“puh-TEE”] says that the molar heat capacity of many solid elements is about three times this constant, roughly 25 joules per mole per kelvin. For an ideal monatomic gas, the molar heat capacity at constant volume is three-halves of this constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, which appears in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: Mayer’s relation says that for an ideal gas, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is larger than the one at constant volume by exactly this constant. This constant has the same units as molar entropy: joules per mole per kelvin.
tossups.r: Dividing this constant by Avogadro’s number gives the Boltzmann constant. For 10 points, name this constant in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: In the Nernst equation, this constant times the temperature, divided by Faraday’s constant, gives a voltage of about 25.7 millivolts at 25 degrees Celsius. That combination tells how a cell’s voltage changes as the concentrations of its chemicals change.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, equal to about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, which also appears in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: The standard Gibbs free energy change of a reaction equals the negative of this constant times the absolute temperature times the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant. This constant also links the equilibrium constants written with pressures and with concentrations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 0.0821 liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin, which appears in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: On an Arrhenius [“ar-RAY-nee-us”] plot, the natural log of a rate constant is graphed against one over the absolute temperature, giving a line whose slope is the negative of the activation energy divided by this constant.
tossups.r: Multiplying this constant by temperature and moles gives pressure times volume for an ideal gas. For 10 points, name this constant.

tossups.p: Jacobus van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”], winner of the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry, showed that osmotic pressure equals a solution’s molarity times this constant times the absolute temperature. That formula has the same form as a gas law first stated by Émile Clapeyron in 1834.
tossups.r: That gas law is the ideal gas law. For 10 points, name this constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin.

tossups.p: The root-mean-square speed of gas molecules is the square root of a fraction: three times this constant times the temperature, divided by the molar mass. That formula shows why light helium atoms move much faster than heavy xenon atoms at the same temperature.
tossups.r: It is about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin. For 10 points, name this constant, which equals Avogadro’s number times the Boltzmann constant.

tossups.p: Chemists pick the value of this constant that matches their pressure units. With pressures in torr, or millimeters of mercury, it is about 62.4 liter-torr per mole per kelvin, because one atmosphere equals 760 torr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this universal constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, from the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: Because this constant has the same value for every ideal gas, equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure hold the same number of molecules. Amedeo Avogadro first proposed that rule in 1811.
tossups.r: It equals about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin. For 10 points, name this constant that appears in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: Since the 2019 redefinition of SI units, this constant has had an exact value, because it is the product of two constants that were fixed exactly: Avogadro’s number and the Boltzmann constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant that appears in the ideal gas law, written pressure times volume equals moles times this constant times temperature.

tossups.p: The Clausius–Clapeyron [“KLOW-zee-us klah-pay-RAWN”] equation, which predicts how a liquid’s vapor pressure rises with temperature, divides the heat of vaporization by this constant. A plot of the natural log of vapor pressure against one over temperature has a slope equal to the negative of that ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, which also appears in the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: Johannes van der Waals’s equation for real gases adds a constant a for attractions between molecules and a constant b for the space the molecules themselves take up, but it still multiplies moles and temperature by this third constant.
tossups.r: Because it is the same for every ideal gas, this constant is often called “universal.” For 10 points, name this constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin.

tossups.p: Using this constant, chemists calculate that one mole of any ideal gas at 0 °C and 1 atmosphere fills about 22.4 liters. Rearranging the same law lets chemists find a gas’s molar mass from its density.
tossups.r: It appears in the ideal gas law. For 10 points, name this constant, about 0.0821 liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin.

tossups.p: For a fixed amount of gas, pressure times volume divided by absolute temperature stays the same, a rule called the combined gas law; that ratio equals the number of moles times this constant. Temperatures must be in kelvins when this constant is used.
tossups.r: It appears in the ideal gas law. For 10 points, name this constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin.

tossups.p: This constant has the same number in joules per mole per kelvin as in kilopascal-liters per mole per kelvin, because one kilopascal times one liter equals exactly one joule. In calories, it is close to 2 per mole per kelvin.
tossups.r: In liter-atmospheres per mole per kelvin, it is about 0.0821. For 10 points, name this constant from the ideal gas law.
