trap.title: Not Boltzmann or Avogadro
trap.body: Three constants are tied together here: this one equals Avogadro’s number times the Boltzmann constant. The Boltzmann constant, about 1.38 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin, does the same job for a single molecule, so answering with it is wrong. The ideal gas law is also a separate answer from the constant inside it.
trap.fix: “Per mole,” 8.314, 0.0821, and the ideal gas law mean the gas constant, R. “Per molecule” or “per particle,” 1.38 × 10⁻²³, and Boltzmann’s tombstone mean the Boltzmann constant; 6.02 × 10²³ means Avogadro’s number. If the question asks for “this law” or “this equation,” say the ideal gas law instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gas constant (accept R, ideal gas constant, universal gas constant, or molar gas constant; do not accept “Boltzmann constant” or “Avogadro’s number”)

topics.name: Reaction rate
topics.kicker: How fast reactants become products · Sped up by heat and catalysts
topics.briefing: A reaction rate tells how fast reactants turn into products, such as how quickly an iron nail rusts or a glow stick fades. Collision theory explains it: molecules must bump into each other hard enough and in the right direction to react. Heating things up, raising concentrations, grinding solids into powder, and adding a catalyst all make reactions go faster.
topics.answerHtml: Reaction rate (accept rate of reaction or speed of reaction; prompt on rate or chemical kinetics; do not accept “rate constant,” “activation energy,” or “catalyst”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Manfred Eigen, Ronald Norrish, and George Porter shared the 1967 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for measuring this quantity for extremely fast reactions, using methods such as flash photolysis. Ahmed Zewail later used laser pulses lasting femtoseconds to watch bonds break during reactions.
tossups.r: Raising the temperature usually increases it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the speed at which reactants turn into products.

tossups.p: Cyril Hinshelwood and Nikolay Semenov shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying the steps of chemical reactions, including branching chain reactions in which this quantity climbs so fast that the mixture explodes.
tossups.r: The branch of chemistry called kinetics studies this quantity. For 10 points, name this measure of how fast a chemical reaction goes.

tossups.p: In 1850, Ludwig Wilhelmy [“vil-HEL-mee”] made one of the first careful measurements of this quantity by tracking how acid broke down table sugar, and he found that it was proportional to the amount of sugar left. That made the sugar’s breakdown a first-order process.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit of time.

tossups.p: In the iodine clock reaction, first studied by Hans Landolt in 1886, a clear solution suddenly turns dark blue after a delay, and students time that delay to compare this quantity at different concentrations and temperatures. Starch makes the blue color once enough iodine forms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which tells how quickly reactants are used up in a chemical reaction.

tossups.p: In the “disappearing cross” experiment, sodium thiosulfate reacts with hydrochloric acid to form cloudy sulfur, and students time how long it takes for an X drawn under the flask to vanish. A shorter time means a larger value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how fast a chemical reaction happens, which increases with higher temperature or concentration.

tossups.p: The exponents in the law for this quantity, called orders, must be found by experiment rather than read from a balanced equation. It is often measured in moles per liter per second, and when it is found from a reactant, a minus sign keeps it positive.
tossups.r: Catalysts increase it. For 10 points, name this quantity, the speed at which reactants turn into products.

tossups.p: If this quantity is proportional to the concentration of just one reactant, the reaction is first-order, and its half-life stays the same no matter how much reactant there is. Radioactive decay follows that pattern. If it does not depend on concentration at all, the reaction is zero-order.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which tells how fast reactants are used up and products form.

tossups.p: In a reaction that happens in several steps, the slowest step acts like a bottleneck and sets this quantity for the whole reaction. That step usually has the highest energy barrier, or activation energy. Speeding up any faster step barely changes this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, how fast reactants become products, which collision theory explains.

tossups.p: Flour dust and coal dust can explode, even though a pile of either burns slowly, because grinding a solid into tiny particles gives it far more surface area. Crushing an antacid tablet before dropping it into water has the same effect on this quantity.
tossups.r: Raising the temperature also increases it. For 10 points, name this quantity, which tells how fast a chemical reaction goes.

tossups.p: Food spoils more slowly in a refrigerator, and a glow stick placed in a freezer glows dimmer but lasts longer, because cooling lowers this quantity. A common rule of thumb says that, for many reactions, this quantity roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which collision theory explains, the speed at which reactants turn into products.

tossups.p: A strip of magnesium ribbon fizzes faster in more concentrated hydrochloric acid, because more acid particles collide with the metal each second. Students often measure this quantity by collecting the hydrogen gas in a syringe and recording its volume every few seconds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the change in the amount of a reactant or product over time.

tossups.p: The Michaelis–Menten [“mih-KAY-lis MEN-ten”] equation, published by Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten in 1913, describes how this quantity for an enzyme levels off at a maximum as more substrate is added. Enzymes and other catalysts raise this quantity by lowering the activation energy.
tossups.r: Collision theory explains it. For 10 points, name this quantity, how fast reactants turn into products.

tossups.p: On a graph of a reactant’s concentration against time, this quantity at any moment equals the steepness of a line tangent to the curve. Because the curve flattens as the reactant is used up, this quantity usually decreases as the reaction goes on.
tossups.r: Catalysts and higher temperatures increase it. For 10 points, name this quantity, which tells how fast a chemical reaction happens.

tossups.p: According to collision theory, only a tiny fraction of the collisions between molecules lead to a reaction, because the molecules must hit with enough energy and in the right orientation. Anything that makes useful collisions happen more often raises this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the speed at which reactants are turned into products.

tossups.p: Cato Guldberg and Peter Waage’s [“VAW-gehz”] law of mass action, from 1864, linked this quantity to the concentrations of the reacting substances. Twenty years later, Jacobus van ’t Hoff [“vahnt HOFF”] wrote _Studies in Chemical Dynamics_, a founding work in the study of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which collision theory explains and which increases with temperature.

clues.t: How fast reactants turn into products: the change in concentration over time
Raised by higher temperature, higher concentration, more surface area, and catalysts
Collision theory explains it: particles must collide with enough energy and in the right orientation
Catalysts, such as enzymes, increase it by lowering the activation energy
Studied in the branch of chemistry called kinetics
Often measured in moles per liter per second; a minus sign keeps it positive when it is found from a reactant
Rule of thumb: for many reactions, it roughly doubles with every 10 °C rise in temperature
Cooling lowers it: food spoils more slowly in a refrigerator, and a glow stick lasts longer in a freezer
Powders react faster than lumps: flour and coal dust can explode, and crushed antacid tablets fizz faster
Magnesium ribbon fizzes faster in more concentrated hydrochloric acid; the hydrogen can be collected in a syringe
In its law, the exponents, called orders, must be found by experiment, not read from the balanced equation
First-order reactions have a constant half-life, as in radioactive decay; zero-order ones don’t depend on concentration at all
The slowest step of a multistep reaction is a bottleneck that sets it for the whole reaction
At any moment, it equals the steepness of a tangent line on a graph of concentration against time
Manfred Eigen, Ronald Norrish, and George Porter shared the 1967 Nobel Prize for studying extremely fast reactions, using flash photolysis
Ahmed Zewail (1999 Nobel Prize) used femtosecond laser pulses to watch bonds break during reactions
Cyril Hinshelwood and Nikolay Semenov shared the 1956 Nobel Prize, studying chain reactions that can speed up until they explode
Ludwig Wilhelmy measured it in 1850 for acid breaking down table sugar, finding it proportional to the sugar left
In Hans Landolt’s iodine clock reaction (1886), a clear solution suddenly turns dark blue after a delay that students time
“Disappearing cross”: sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid make cloudy sulfur that hides an X drawn under the flask
The Michaelis–Menten equation (1913) shows an enzyme’s value leveling off at a maximum as more substrate is added
Guldberg and Waage’s law of mass action (1864) tied it to concentrations; van ’t Hoff wrote _Studies in Chemical Dynamics_ (1884)

trap.title: Quantity, not the factor
trap.body: Tossups on this quantity are packed with the things that change it, so players blurt “catalyst,” “temperature,” “activation energy,” or “collision theory,” which are separate answers. The “rate constant,” k, and the “rate law” are also different answers: they are pieces of the math, not the speed itself. Saying just “rate” or “kinetics” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this quantity,” the speed at which reactants become products, say reaction rate. “These substances” that speed reactions up are catalysts; “this energy barrier” is activation energy; “this theory” about colliding particles is collision theory; “this constant” in an equation is the rate constant.
trap.line: Real answer line: Reaction rate (accept rate of reaction or speed of reaction; prompt on rate or chemical kinetics; do not accept “rate constant,” “activation energy,” or “catalyst”)

topics.name: Dipoles
topics.kicker: Separated positive and negative charge · Why water molecules stick together
topics.dates: Debye won a Nobel for studying them, 1936
topics.briefing: A dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges, or poles, separated by a distance, like a tiny bar magnet made of electric charge. Water molecules are dipoles because their bent shape leaves the oxygen end slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive, which is why water molecules cling together and why a microwave oven can heat food by twisting them back and forth. Chemists measure dipole moments in debyes, named for Peter Debye.
topics.answerHtml: Dipoles (accept dipole moments; accept electric or magnetic dipoles; prompt on polar molecules or polarity; do not accept “dipole–dipole forces”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Peter Debye [“duh-BYE”] won the 1936 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for measuring the moments of these entities in molecules, and a unit for those moments, equal to about 3.34 times 10 to the minus 30 coulomb-meters, is named for him. A water molecule’s moment is about 1.85 of those units.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pairs of equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance, found in polar molecules.

tossups.p: Chemists draw one of these as an arrow with a small plus sign crossing its tail, pointing toward the more electronegative atom, while physicists usually point the arrow the other way, from negative to positive. For a molecule, the moment of one of these is measured in debyes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, found in polar molecules like water.

tossups.p: In a uniform electric field, one of these feels no net force but does feel a torque that tries to line it up with the field. Its moment equals the size of either charge multiplied by the distance between the two charges.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pairs of equal and opposite charges, which polar molecules such as water have.

tossups.p: Far from one of these, its electric field weakens with the cube of the distance, faster than the inverse-square field of a single charge, because the fields of its two opposite charges nearly cancel. Placing two of these back to back makes a quadrupole.
tossups.r: Polar molecules like water are examples. For 10 points, name these pairs of equal and opposite charges separated by a distance.

tossups.p: Heinrich Hertz proved that radio waves exist in the late 1880s, using a spark gap between two metal rods, an antenna design named for these things. Old “rabbit ears” TV antennas used the same design, with two rods pointing in opposite directions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pairs of opposite charges or poles, which also describe polar molecules like water.

tossups.p: A microwave oven heats food because its rapidly flipping electric field, which changes direction billions of times per second, makes water molecules twist back and forth to line up with it. Those molecules respond because each one is one of these.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, found in polar molecules.

tossups.p: Water’s dielectric constant, about 80 at room temperature, is unusually high because its molecules are strong examples of these and turn to partly cancel an outside electric field. That ability helps water pull apart the ions in salts, so salts dissolve well in it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of charge, measured in debyes, that make a molecule polar.

tossups.p: The cis isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene [“dye-klor-oh-ETH-een”] has an overall one of these, but the trans isomer does not, because its two carbon–chlorine bonds point in opposite directions and cancel. Each of those polar bonds is a small one of these.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, whose moments are measured in debyes.

tossups.p: Carbon dioxide has none of these overall, because it is a straight, linear molecule and the pulls of its two polar bonds cancel. Carbon tetrachloride also lacks one, because its four bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron.
tossups.r: Water has one because its molecule is bent. For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, which make molecules polar.

tossups.p: Ammonia has one of these because its lone pair gives it a trigonal pyramidal shape, but boron trifluoride, a flat triangle, has none. Molecules with lopsided shapes and unequal sharing of electrons usually have one of these.
tossups.r: Polar molecules like water have them. For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, measured in debyes.

tossups.p: Acetone and butane have almost the same molar mass, but acetone boils at about 56 °C while butane boils near 0 °C, because acetone molecules are examples of these and attract one another more strongly. Butane molecules feel only weak London dispersion forces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, found in polar molecules.

tossups.p: Willem Keesom [“KAY-sum”] described the attraction between two permanent examples of these, and Peter Debye described the attraction between a permanent one and one that it induces in a neighbor. Fritz London explained the attraction between temporary ones that flicker in electron clouds.
tossups.r: Water molecules have them. For 10 points, name these pairs of opposite partial charges, found in polar molecules.

tossups.p: No one has ever confirmed finding an isolated north or south magnetic pole, called a monopole, so even the smallest magnet is one of these. Earth’s magnetic field is roughly shaped like that of a giant magnetic one of these.
tossups.r: A bar magnet is one. For 10 points, name these pairs of opposite poles or charges, which also describe polar molecules such as water.

tossups.p: When a charged object comes near a nonpolar atom, it can push the atom’s electron cloud to one side, creating a temporary, induced example of one of these. Big atoms with loose electron clouds, like xenon, are especially easy to distort this way, a property called polarizability.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pairs of equal and opposite charges, which permanently exist in polar molecules like water.

tossups.p: When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, the bond becomes one of these, with partial charges written with the Greek letter delta. Substances made of molecules with these tend to dissolve in one another, a rule summed up as “like dissolves like.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these separations of positive and negative charge, which make molecules like water polar.

clues.t: A pair of equal and opposite charges, or poles, separated by a distance
Polar molecules have them; water is the classic example
Water has one because its bent shape (about 104.5°) leaves the oxygen end slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive
Their moments are measured in debyes, named for Peter Debye
The moment equals charge times the distance between the charges; it is a vector, so bond moments can add up or cancel
A difference in electronegativity gives a bond partial charges (δ+ and δ−), making the bond one
Linear carbon dioxide has no overall one because its two polar bonds cancel; tetrahedral carbon tetrachloride has none either
Trigonal pyramidal ammonia has one; flat, triangular boron trifluoride has none
Microwave ovens heat food by making water molecules twist back and forth in a rapidly flipping electric field
“Like dissolves like”: substances whose molecules have them tend to dissolve in one another
Attractions between them raise boiling points: acetone boils at about 56 °C, but butane, of nearly the same mass, boils near 0 °C
Hydrogen bonds are an especially strong attraction between them
A bar magnet is a magnetic one; no isolated magnetic pole, or monopole, has ever been confirmed
In a uniform electric field, one feels no net force but feels a torque that lines it up with the field
Peter Debye won the 1936 Nobel Prize in Chemistry partly for measuring their moments; one debye is about 3.34 × 10⁻³⁰ coulomb-meters
A water molecule’s moment is about 1.85 debyes
Chemists draw them as arrows with a plus sign on the tail, pointing toward the more electronegative atom; physicists point the other way
Far away, the field of one weakens with the cube of the distance; two placed back to back make a quadrupole
Heinrich Hertz proved radio waves exist in the late 1880s with an antenna design named for them; “rabbit ears” TV antennas use it
Water’s dielectric constant, about 80, is high because its molecules turn to partly cancel an outside field
cis-1,2-Dichloroethene has an overall one, but in the trans isomer the opposite carbon–chlorine bonds cancel
Keesom: attraction between two permanent ones; Debye: a permanent one and an induced one; London: temporary ones in electron clouds
A nearby charge can push an electron cloud aside, inducing a temporary one; big atoms like xenon are easy to distort (polarizability)
Earth’s magnetic field is roughly shaped like that of a giant magnetic one

trap.title: The charges, not the forces
trap.body: Dipoles cause several intermolecular forces with their own answer lines: dipole–dipole forces, hydrogen bonds, and London dispersion forces, which act between temporary dipoles. Answering “dipole–dipole forces” when the question wants the charge separation itself is wrong, and so is “electronegativity,” the property that creates polar bonds. Saying only “polar molecule” or “polarity” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these” pairs of separated positive and negative charge, measured in debyes, say dipoles or dipole moment. “These attractions” or “these forces” between molecules want the force’s name, and “this property” of an atom pulling on shared electrons is electronegativity.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dipoles (accept dipole moments; accept electric or magnetic dipoles; prompt on polar molecules or polarity; do not accept “dipole–dipole forces”)

topics.name: Molecular orbital theory
topics.kicker: Electrons spread over whole molecules · Why oxygen sticks to a magnet
topics.briefing: Molecular orbital theory pictures a molecule’s electrons spread out over the whole molecule instead of sitting in bonds between pairs of atoms. Electrons in low-energy bonding orbitals hold the atoms together, while those in high-energy antibonding orbitals weaken the bond. The theory explains something simpler bonding pictures miss: liquid oxygen sticks to a magnet, because each oxygen molecule has two unpaired electrons.
topics.answerHtml: Molecular orbital theory (accept MO theory or Hund–Mulliken theory; accept molecular orbitals; prompt on orbital theory or LCAO; do not accept “valence bond theory” or “atomic orbitals”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While developing this theory, Robert Mulliken coined the word “orbital” in 1932. Its main rival, the valence bond approach championed by Linus Pauling, pictures bonds as overlapping orbitals on neighboring atoms, while this theory lets each electron spread over the whole molecule.
tossups.r: Mulliken won the 1966 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. For 10 points, name this theory that sorts electrons into bonding and antibonding orbitals.

tossups.p: In the late 1920s, Friedrich Hund [“HOONT”] and Robert Mulliken developed this theory, which treats each electron as spread over the whole molecule instead of belonging to a single bond. In 1927, Walter Heitler and Fritz London explained the hydrogen molecule with a competing approach, valence bond theory.
tossups.r: It sorts electrons into bonding and antibonding orbitals. For 10 points, name this theory of bonding that explains why oxygen is attracted to magnets.

tossups.p: In 1929, John Lennard-Jones proposed building the orbitals of this theory by adding and subtracting atomic orbitals, a method called the linear combination of atomic orbitals. Adding two atomic orbitals together makes a lower-energy orbital, and subtracting them makes a higher-energy one.
tossups.r: Those orbitals are called bonding and antibonding. For 10 points, name this theory of chemical bonding.

tossups.p: This theory explains why the bond order of oxygen drops from 2 in the oxygen molecule to 1.5 in the superoxide ion and 1 in the peroxide ion: each added electron goes into an antibonding orbital. Removing an electron instead raises the bond order to 2.5.
tossups.r: This theory also explains why liquid oxygen clings to a strong magnet. For 10 points, name this theory of bonding.

tossups.p: In a classic demonstration, liquid nitrogen poured between the poles of a strong magnet flows straight through, because this theory gives nitrogen’s molecule a bond order of 3 with every electron paired. That bond order matches the triple bond in nitrogen’s Lewis structure.
tossups.r: Liquid oxygen, by contrast, sticks to the magnet. For 10 points, name this theory, which explains that difference with bonding and antibonding orbitals.

tossups.p: In this theory, a molecule’s bond order equals half the difference between its number of bonding electrons and its number of antibonding electrons. That formula gives two helium atoms a bond order of zero, explaining why helium atoms do not pair up into ordinary molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of bonding that sorts electrons into orbitals spread over a whole molecule.

tossups.p: In diagrams for this theory, higher-energy orbitals are marked with an asterisk and have a node, a region with no chance of finding an electron, between the two nuclei. Filling those orbitals weakens a bond.
tossups.r: Lower-energy orbitals, which pile electrons between the nuclei, are called bonding orbitals. For 10 points, name this theory of chemical bonding.

tossups.p: This theory says that combining any number of atomic orbitals always produces the same number of new orbitals, some lower in energy and some higher. Electrons fill the new orbitals from the bottom up, following Hund’s rule and the Pauli exclusion principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of bonding that explains why oxygen is attracted to magnets.

tossups.p: This theory gives nitric oxide, a molecule with an odd number of electrons, a bond order of 2.5 and one unpaired electron, so the gas is weakly attracted to a magnet. Removing that lone electron makes the nitrosonium [“ny-troh-SOH-nee-um”] ion, whose bond order rises to 3.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory in which electrons occupy bonding and antibonding orbitals spread over a whole molecule.

tossups.p: This theory calls a molecule’s highest occupied orbital and lowest unoccupied orbital its frontier orbitals, and the energy gap between them helps decide what color of light the molecule absorbs. Long chains of alternating double bonds, like the one in beta-carotene, have small gaps, so they absorb visible light.
tossups.r: It sorts electrons into bonding and antibonding orbitals. For 10 points, name this theory of chemical bonding developed by Robert Mulliken.

tossups.p: Erich Hückel [“HOO-kul”] used a simplified version of this theory to show that flat rings with 4n + 2 pi electrons, such as benzene, are especially stable. In that version, benzene’s six pi electrons spread around the whole ring instead of sitting in three separate double bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of bonding that also explains why oxygen is attracted to magnets.

tossups.p: When this theory is applied to a metal, the orbitals of huge numbers of atoms merge into nearly continuous energy bands, and electrons moving through partly filled bands carry current. The size of the gap between bands separates insulators from semiconductors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of chemical bonding, which describes bonding and antibonding orbitals spread over whole molecules.

tossups.p: Photoelectron spectroscopy, which measures the energy needed to knock electrons out of a molecule, supports this theory by showing electrons at the separate energy levels it predicts. This theory explains why the hydrogen molecule ion, with just one electron, still holds together with a bond order of one-half.
tossups.r: It explains why oxygen is attracted to magnets. For 10 points, name this theory of bonding that sorts electrons into bonding and antibonding orbitals.

tossups.p: This theory builds sigma orbitals from atomic orbitals that overlap head-on along the line between two nuclei and pi orbitals from p orbitals that overlap side by side. In the oxygen molecule, the two highest-energy electrons sit unpaired in a pair of pi-star orbitals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory that explains oxygen’s attraction to magnets with bonding and antibonding orbitals.

tossups.p: Kenichi Fukui’s [“foo-KOO-eez”] frontier orbital ideas and the Woodward–Hoffmann rules both use this theory to predict whether ring-forming reactions such as the Diels–Alder reaction can happen. Fukui shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Roald Hoffmann.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this theory of bonding in which electrons spread over a whole molecule in bonding and antibonding orbitals.

Sigma orbitals come from head-on overlap; pi orbitals come from p orbitals overlapping side by side
Electrons fill its orbitals from the bottom up, following Hund’s rule and the Pauli exclusion principle
Its competitor was valence bond theory, championed by Linus Pauling
Frontier orbitals: the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals; the gap between them affects what color a molecule absorbs
Mulliken also coined the word “orbital” in 1932
Friedrich Hund and Robert Mulliken developed it in the late 1920s
In 1927, Walter Heitler and Fritz London explained the hydrogen molecule with the competing valence bond approach
In 1929, John Lennard-Jones built its orbitals by adding and subtracting atomic orbitals, a linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO)
Oxygen’s bond order is 2; the superoxide ion’s is 1.5, the peroxide ion’s is 1, and removing an electron gives 2.5
Nitric oxide, with an odd number of electrons, has a bond order of 2.5 and is weakly magnetic; the nitrosonium ion has a bond order of 3
Long chains of alternating double bonds, as in beta-carotene, have small gaps and absorb visible light
Erich Hückel used a simple version to show that flat rings with 4n + 2 pi electrons, like benzene, are especially stable

trap.title: Molecular, not atomic
trap.body: Atomic orbitals belong to one atom, while this theory’s orbitals spread over a whole molecule, so “atomic orbitals” is a different answer. The competing valence bond theory, championed by Linus Pauling, describes bonds as overlapping orbitals on neighboring atoms, and VSEPR theory only predicts shapes. Neither of those explains why oxygen sticks to a magnet.
trap.fix: Bonding and antibonding orbitals, bond order, oxygen’s magnetism, Mulliken, and sigma-star or pi-star orbitals mean molecular orbital theory. One atom’s s, p, d, and f regions mean atomic orbitals; hybrid orbitals and resonance mean valence bond theory; electron pairs pushing apart to set a shape mean VSEPR.
trap.line: Real answer line: Molecular orbital theory (accept MO theory or Hund–Mulliken theory; accept molecular orbitals; prompt on orbital theory or LCAO; do not accept “valence bond theory” or “atomic orbitals”)
